The surgical task is to separate the gallbladder from its attachment to the liver, which defines the correct plane of dissection. The safe region is a narrow, vertically oriented area in the center-left of the image. This zone represents the correct surgical plane—the avascular, areolar tissue plane—between the gallbladder wall and the liver capsule. The surgical instrument, a hook dissector, is correctly positioned within this safe plane, actively separating the gallbladder. Dissection should be confined to this specific plane to safely peel the gallbladder away from the liver.

The unsafe region is extensive and comprises two main areas. The first is the large expanse of liver parenchyma, which covers the entire top portion and right side of the image. Dissecting into the liver tissue is unsafe as it will cause significant bleeding and is not part of the procedure. The second unsafe area is the deeper tissue inferior and medial to the current point of dissection, located in the lower-center of the view. This region contains unexposed fatty and connective tissue that likely hides the critical structures of the hepatocystic triangle (Calot's triangle), including the cystic artery and cystic duct. Dissection in this area without clear identification of these structures carries a high risk of bile duct injury or major vascular injury.
